title: Ben Gvir Enters Al-Aqsa Compound on Tisha B'Av, Praises Jewish Prayer
excerpt: Israel's far-right police minister visited the sensitive Jerusalem holy site on the Jewish day of mourning, drawing condemnation from Jordan and Palestinian officials for breaching the decades-old status quo on non-Muslim worship.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ben-Gvir's visit to Al-Aqsa on Tisha B'Av breached the status quo allowing only Muslim worship.
  • Jordan condemned the visit as a barbaric act and unacceptable provocation against the mosque's sanctity.
  • In June 2026, there were 26 incursions into Al-Aqsa, with over 4,200 Israeli settlers entering.
  • India faces diplomatic pressure as Gulf communities monitor rising tensions at Al-Aqsa.

Ben-Gvir Enters Compound, Praises Jewish Prayer

Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir visited the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in Jerusalem's Old City on Thursday, July 23, coinciding with Tisha B'Av — the annual Jewish day of fasting and mourning commemorating the destruction of the ancient temples.

https://x.com/QudsNen/status/2080202277499875663

In a video distributed by his office, Ben-Gvir praised what he described as Jewish worshippers praying at the site, in direct breach of the decades-old status quo arrangement that permits only Muslim prayer at the compound.

"On Tisha B'Av we mark the destruction. But we also see huge progress on the Temple Mount. Look at what's happening here — Jews praying, feeling like they're the owners of the place. This has never happened before."

— Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's National Security Minister

The video appeared to show at least one Jewish visitor bowing in prayer inside the compound. Thousands of Israelis entered the site under police protection throughout the day, with many reportedly praying, singing, and dancing in the courtyards. No immediate unrest was reported.

Status Quo and Why It Matters

The Al-Aqsa Mosque compound — known to Jews as the Temple Mount — sits atop a hillside in Jerusalem's walled Old City. It is the most sacred site in Judaism and Islam's third-holiest, housing both the Dome of the Rock and the Al-Aqsa Mosque.

Under a delicate arrangement maintained since 1967 with Muslim authorities, the compound is administered by a Jordanian religious foundation known as the Waqf. Jewish visitors are permitted to enter during designated hours but are prohibited from praying there. Israel's official policy accepts this arrangement.

Attempts to alter the rules have historically triggered violent confrontations. The compound was a flashpoint during the 2021 clashes that preceded the 11-day Gaza war, and restrictions on Palestinian access have tightened considerably in recent years.

International Condemnation

Jordan's foreign ministry condemned Ben-Gvir's visit as "a desecration of the sanctity of the mosque, an escalation, a barbaric act, and unacceptable provocation," describing it as a violation of the status quo agreement.

The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Affairs also condemned the incursion. The Palestinian Authority presidency has consistently described such visits as blatant violations of the historical and legal status quo at the site.

There was no immediate comment from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office. In previous instances, Netanyahu has issued statements affirming that Israel's policy of maintaining the status quo "has not changed and will not change" — though critics note the gap between stated policy and what unfolds on the ground under Ben-Gvir's watch.

An Escalating Pattern

Thursday's visit is part of a broader escalation at the holy site. According to a report by the Palestinian Ministry of Awqaf and Religious Affairs, Israeli forces carried out 26 incursions into the Al-Aqsa compound in June 2026 alone, with over 4,200 Israeli settlers entering through the Mughrabi Gate that month.

Ben-Gvir has entered the compound at least 16 times since joining Netanyahu's government in late 2022. Under his direction as police minister, Israeli officers have increasingly allowed Jewish visitors to pray, sing, and prostrate at the site — a significant departure from enforcement of the status quo.

The compound was closed to the public for 40 days following Israel's military strikes on Iran in February 2026. Israeli authorities also prevented Eid al-Fitr prayers at Al-Aqsa this year — the first such restriction since the 1967 occupation of East Jerusalem.

Jerusalem's Grand Mufti, Sheikh Mohammed Hussein, was recently detained and barred from entering the compound for one week after delivering Friday prayers — a measure that drew further condemnation from Palestinian officials.

India's Tightrope Walk

The recurring tensions at Al-Aqsa put India's carefully calibrated Middle East diplomacy under renewed strain. New Delhi maintains strong defense and technology ties with Israel while simultaneously supporting Palestinian statehood at the United Nations.

For the estimated eight million Indians working across Gulf states — particularly in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait — Al-Aqsa is a deeply sensitive issue. Gulf governments have historically viewed provocations at the holy site with alarm, and any escalation that prompts diplomatic fallout could affect the environment for Indian workers and businesses in the region.

India's Ministry of External Affairs has not commented on Thursday's incident. In the past, New Delhi has called for maintaining the status quo at holy sites in Jerusalem while avoiding direct criticism of specific Israeli actions.

What Comes Next

With Tisha B'Av observed annually and Ben-Gvir showing no sign of curtailing his provocative visits, the pattern of confrontation at Al-Aqsa appears set to continue. Netanyahu's silence on the matter leaves open questions about whether his coalition partner's actions represent a deliberate policy shift or a political liability the prime minister chooses to tolerate.

The coming days will reveal whether Thursday's visit triggers broader regional reactions beyond Jordan's condemnation. In previous cycles, Al-Aqsa provocations have served as catalysts for wider unrest — a risk that grows with each escalation.
